exchanges: Hi! I just arrived in Montreal yesterday for my master's. Still jet-lagged and a little overwhelmed.
Welcome to Montreal! Being overwhelmed the first few days is normal; it usually eases once you have a routine.
The apartment is small but nice. It's in Rosemont, on the second floor of a duplex.
Rosemont is a lovely area, lots of parks and cafés. Duplex living is very Montreal.
My landlord lives downstairs. Her name is Lena and she's very kind. She brought me a plate of pierogi.
That's a warm welcome. A landlord who lives on site and cooks is a good sign.
She's a retired pharmacist, so she also gave me a long speech about drinking water and sleeping properly.
Sounds like she's adopted you a little. Not bad advice for jet lag either.
Ha, yes. She also has a tortoise named Boris who wanders around the backyard.
That's a very charming detail. I hope Boris is friendly.
Tomorrow I meet my supervisor, Professor Adeyemi. I'm nervous because I've only spoken to her on video.
First in-person meetings can feel bigger than they are. She chose you for the program, so she's already on your side.
The meeting went well! She introduced me to the lab. There are four of us.
Great to hear. Did you get along with the others?
Mostly. There's Yusuf, who's from Ankara, and he's been very helpful with the equipment.
Having someone patient show you the equipment makes a big difference early on.
There's also another Lena in the lab, which is confusing. She's from Hamburg.
Two Lenas in your daily life will take some getting used to. Maybe 'lab Lena' and 'landlord Lena' for now.
That's exactly what I've been calling them in my head. Lab Lena has a parrot who apparently says 'bonjour' to everyone.
A bilingual bird, very fitting for Montreal.
My knee has been bothering me since the flight. I think it's from sitting cramped for so long.
Long flights can definitely aggravate joints. If it doesn't settle in a few days, it'd be worth getting it looked at.
The university has a sports clinic, so I booked a physiotherapy appointment.
That's a good use of student services. Physios are great at figuring out mechanical issues.
The physio, Mr. Gagnon, said it's tendinitis, probably from running on the treadmill before I left.
That's usually manageable with rest and the right exercises. Did he give you a plan?
Yes, some stretches and no running for three weeks. I'm annoyed.
Three weeks feels long, but it's much shorter than dealing with a chronic injury.
Lab Lena invited us to her place for dinner on Friday. She has to cook gluten-free because she has celiac disease, so she's doing a big rice dish.
That's a nice way to get the lab together. Rice dishes are great for a crowd.
I need to correct something I told you: Yusuf isn't from Ankara. He did his master's there, but he grew up in Izmir.
Thanks for clarifying. A coastal hometown, then; he might find the river here familiar.
He laughed when I got it wrong; apparently everyone assumes that.
It's an easy assumption when someone's studied there. He sounds good-natured about it.
Professor Adeyemi gave me my first reading list. It's twenty papers.
That's a solid start. Skimming abstracts first can help you prioritize.
Good idea. I'm going to do that this weekend.
A quiet weekend with coffee and papers sounds like a reasonable plan.
Dinner at Lab Lena's was fun. The parrot did say bonjour.
Glad it lived up to the reputation. Sounds like a good night.
I also signed up for French classes at the community centre. Mine is terrible.
Classes plus daily practice here will improve it quickly.
My brother Kenji called this morning. He's in Toronto and he's finally got a job he loves.
That's great news. What's he doing?
He's a sommelier now, at a restaurant on King Street. He's been studying wine for years.
All that studying paid off. He must be thrilled.
He is. He promised to visit in December.
That'll be something to look forward to during the cold months.

questions.message: What did the physio diagnose my knee with?
Yusuf's hometown is Izmir, isn't it?
Does Professor Adeyemi have any pets?
I should find a good restaurant to take him to when he's here.
